facts.text: At 9 to 11 cm long, the Scarlet Honeyeater is the smallest honeyeater in Australia.
facts.quote: At 9 to 11 cm (3.5 to 4.3 in) long, it is the smallest honeyeater in Australia.

facts.text: The male Scarlet Honeyeater is a striking bright red with black wings, while the female is entirely brown.
facts.quote: It is sexually dimorphic; the male is a striking bright red with black wings, while the female is entirely brown.

facts.text: The Scarlet Honeyeater is more vocal than most honeyeaters, with calls including a bell-like tinkling.
facts.quote: The species is more vocal than most honeyeaters, and a variety of calls have been recorded, including a bell-like tinkling.

facts.text: The main call of the Scarlet Honeyeater is a tuneful tinkling made up of sets of six notes that rise or fall in tone.
facts.quote: The main call is a tuneful tinkling call made up of sets of six notes that rise or fall in tone.

facts.text: The Scarlet Honeyeater forages in the crowns of trees, darting from flower to flower and sometimes hovering while probing for nectar.
facts.quote: The scarlet myzomela is arboreal, foraging in the crowns of trees, darting from flower to flower, probing for nectar with its long curved bill.

facts.text: Breeding New Holland honeyeaters actively drive off Scarlet Honeyeaters from feeding areas.
facts.quote: In particular, breeding New Holland honeyeaters actively drive off scarlet myzomelas.

facts.text: The female lays two or rarely three flecked white eggs in a 5 cm cup-shaped nest high in a tree.
facts.quote: The female lays two or rarely three flecked white eggs in a 5 cm (2 in) diameter cup-shaped nest high in a tree.

facts.text: The tiny nest of shredded bark and spider web takes around 8 days to build, and both sexes help construct it.
facts.quote: The nest is around 5 cm (2.0 in) in diameter, and takes around 8 days to build before eggs are laid in it. Both sexes build the nest

facts.text: The Scarlet Honeyeater is listed as a species of least concern thanks to its large range and stable population.
facts.quote: listed as being a species of least concern by the IUCN, on account of its large range (1,960,000 square km) and stable population
